title: Excretory Products and Their Elimination
description: Grade 11 Biology: human excretory system and the kidney, urine formation by filtration, reabsorption and secretion, regulation of body water, and kidney disorders including dialysis.

topics.title: Excretion and the Human Excretory System
topics.concept:
As the body carries out its activities, it produces wastes that would be harmful if they built up — especially nitrogen-containing wastes from breaking down proteins. Excretion is the removal of these harmful metabolic wastes from the body. The main nitrogenous waste in humans is urea, which is made in the liver from ammonia and removed by the kidneys. (Animals that excrete mainly urea, like humans, are called ureotelic; those excreting ammonia are ammonotelic, and those excreting uric acid, like birds, are uricotelic.)

The main organ system for excretion in humans is the excretory (urinary) system, which consists of:

  • A pair of bean-shaped kidneys — which filter the blood and make urine.
  • Two ureters — tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
  • The urinary bladder — a muscular bag that stores urine.
  • The urethra — the tube through which urine leaves the body.

Each kidney is made of about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons — the functional units of the kidney. A nephron has a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule enclosing a knot of capillaries (the glomerulus), followed by a long coiled tubule. Besides the kidneys, the lungs remove CO₂ and water vapour, the skin removes salts and water as sweat, and the liver removes some wastes through bile.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is excretion, and what is the main nitrogenous waste in humans?
examples.solution:
Excretion removes harmful wastes.

  • Excretion is the removal of harmful metabolic wastes from the body.
  • The main nitrogenous waste in humans is urea.
examples.answer: Excretion is the removal of harmful metabolic wastes; in humans the main nitrogenous waste is urea.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the four parts of the human urinary system.
examples.solution:
Trace the path of urine.

  • Kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, urethra.
examples.answer: Kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
examples.solution:
The kidney is made of tiny units.

  • The nephron is the functional (filtering) unit of the kidney.

recap:
• Excretion = removal of harmful metabolic wastes; main human waste = urea (made in liver; humans are ureotelic).
  • Urinary system: kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra.
  • Kidney's functional unit = nephron (~1 million per kidney; Bowman's capsule + glomerulus + tubule).
  • Other excretory organs: lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat), liver (bile).

quiz.q: The main nitrogenous waste excreted by humans is:
quiz.explanation: Humans are ureotelic — they mainly excrete urea.

quiz.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
quiz.explanation: The nephron is the kidney's functional filtering unit.

topics.title: Urine Formation and Regulation of Body Water
topics.concept:
The kidneys make urine from the blood in three steps that take place along the nephron:

  • Glomerular filtration — blood under pressure is filtered in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule. Water and small molecules (glucose, salts, urea) pass through into the tubule, while blood cells and large proteins are held back. The filtered liquid is called the glomerular filtrate.
  • Reabsorption (tubular reabsorption) — as the filtrate flows along the tubule, the useful substances the body needs — all the glucose, most of the water, and many salts — are reabsorbed back into the blood. This is why we do not lose valuable nutrients.
  • Secretion (tubular secretion) — some extra wastes and ions (like H⁺ and K⁺) are actively added from the blood into the tubule. What remains is urine.

Out of about 180 litres of filtrate formed each day, only about 1.5 litres become urine — the rest is reabsorbed. The urine then passes to the bladder and is released.

The kidneys also keep the body's water and salt balance steady — a process called osmoregulation. When the body is short of water, a hormone (ADH, the anti-diuretic hormone) makes the kidney reabsorb more water, so the urine is concentrated and small in amount. When there is plenty of water, less ADH is released, so more dilute urine is made. In this way the kidney constantly adjusts how much water to keep and how much to remove, keeping the internal environment stable (homeostasis).

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three steps of urine formation.
examples.solution:
Urine is made along the nephron.

  • Glomerular filtration, reabsorption, and secretion.
examples.answer: Glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, and tubular secretion.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is glucose normally absent from the urine of a healthy person?
examples.solution:
Glucose is recovered.

  • All the glucose in the filtrate is reabsorbed into the blood during reabsorption.
  • So none is left in the urine.
examples.answer: Because all the filtered glucose is reabsorbed into the blood, so none remains in the urine.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does the kidney make the urine more concentrated when the body lacks water?
examples.solution:
A hormone controls water reabsorption.

  • ADH (anti-diuretic hormone) is released.
  • It makes the kidney reabsorb more water, so the urine is concentrated and small in volume.
examples.answer: More ADH is released, causing the kidney to reabsorb more water, so less, more concentrated urine is made.

recap:
• Urine formation: filtration (glomerulus) → reabsorption (glucose, most water, salts back to blood) → secretion (extra wastes/ions added).
  • ~180 L filtrate/day → only ~1.5 L urine.
  • Osmoregulation: kidneys balance water and salts; ADH ↑ → more water reabsorbed (concentrated urine).
  • Keeps the internal environment stable (homeostasis).

quiz.q: The first step of urine formation, in the glomerulus, is:
quiz.explanation: Glomerular filtration is the first step of urine formation.

quiz.q: The hormone that makes the kidney reabsorb more water is:

topics.title: Kidney Disorders and Dialysis
topics.concept:
Because the kidneys filter the blood and control its composition, kidney problems can make harmful wastes build up in the body. Some important kidney disorders:

  • Kidney (renal) failure — the kidneys stop filtering the blood properly, so wastes like urea build up in the blood. It can be sudden (acute) or long-term (chronic).
  • Kidney stones (renal calculi) — hard crystals of salts that form in the kidney, causing severe pain and blocking the flow of urine.
  • Infections of the urinary tract.
  • Presence of glucose or protein in the urine, which can signal diabetes or kidney damage.

When the kidneys fail badly, the blood must be cleaned artificially by a process called dialysis. In haemodialysis, the patient's blood is passed through a machine (an artificial kidney) where it flows past a selectively permeable membrane; wastes such as urea diffuse out into a special dialysing fluid while useful substances are kept, and the cleaned blood is returned to the body. Dialysis keeps a patient alive but must be repeated regularly. The long-term cure for permanent kidney failure is a kidney transplant, in which a healthy kidney from a matched donor replaces the failed one. To keep the kidneys healthy, drink enough water, eat a balanced diet that is not too high in salt or protein, and treat infections promptly.

examples.solution:
The kidneys stop working well.

  • The kidneys cannot filter the blood properly.
  • Wastes like urea build up in the blood.
examples.answer: The kidneys stop filtering the blood properly, so wastes such as urea accumulate in the blood.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is dialysis, and how does it remove wastes?
examples.solution:
Dialysis cleans blood artificially.

  • Blood is passed through a machine across a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Wastes like urea diffuse out into the dialysing fluid, and clean blood is returned.
examples.answer: Dialysis cleans the blood artificially: wastes diffuse out across a membrane into a dialysing fluid, and the clean blood is returned.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the permanent cure for complete kidney failure?
examples.solution:
Dialysis is only a support; a cure replaces the kidney.

  • A kidney transplant from a matched donor.
examples.answer: A kidney transplant from a matched donor.

recap:
• Kidney failure: kidneys cannot filter blood → urea builds up; kidney stones: hard salt crystals, painful, block urine.
  • Dialysis (artificial kidney): wastes diffuse across a membrane into dialysing fluid; clean blood returned; repeated regularly.
  • Permanent cure = kidney transplant (matched donor).
  • Keep kidneys healthy: enough water, balanced low-salt diet, treat infections.

quiz.q: Cleaning the blood artificially when the kidneys fail is called:
quiz.explanation: Dialysis cleans the blood artificially in kidney failure.

quiz.q: Hard crystals of salts that form in the kidney are called:
quiz.explanation: Kidney stones (renal calculi) are hard salt crystals in the kidney.

questions.q: Removal of harmful metabolic wastes from the body is:
questions.explanation: Excretion removes harmful metabolic wastes.

questions.q: The main nitrogenous waste in humans is:
questions.explanation: Humans are ureotelic, excreting mainly urea.

questions.q: Urea is made in the:
questions.explanation: Urea is formed in the liver from ammonia.

questions.q: Tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder are the:
questions.explanation: Ureters carry urine from kidneys to the bladder.

questions.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explanation: The nephron is the kidney's functional unit.

questions.q: The knot of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule is the:
questions.explanation: The glomerulus is the capillary knot where filtration occurs.

questions.q: Besides the kidneys, which organ removes CO₂ and water vapour?
questions.explanation: The lungs excrete CO₂ and water vapour.

questions.q: The first step of urine formation is:
questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration is the first step.

questions.q: During reabsorption, the kidney returns to the blood all of the:
questions.explanation: All filtered glucose is reabsorbed, so none appears in urine.

questions.q: About how much urine is formed daily from ~180 L of filtrate?
questions.explanation: Most filtrate is reabsorbed; only about 1.5 L becomes urine.

questions.q: Balancing the body's water and salt content is called:
questions.explanation: Osmoregulation maintains water and salt balance.

questions.q: When the body lacks water, ADH causes the kidney to:
questions.explanation: ADH increases water reabsorption, concentrating the urine.

questions.q: Hard crystals of salts in the kidney are:
questions.explanation: Kidney stones (renal calculi) are hard salt crystals.

questions.q: Artificial cleaning of blood in kidney failure is:
questions.explanation: Dialysis cleans the blood when the kidneys fail.

questions.q: The permanent cure for complete kidney failure is a:
questions.explanation: A kidney transplant from a matched donor is the lasting cure.

questions.q: Blood cells and large proteins are normally absent from the glomerular filtrate because they:
options: Are too big to pass through the filter
questions.explanation: Filtration holds back large components; only water and small molecules pass into the tubule.

questions.q: Glucose in the urine of a person may indicate diabetes because the filtered glucose:
options: Exceeds what the tubules can reabsorb
questions.explanation: If blood glucose is very high, the tubules cannot reabsorb it all, so some appears in urine.

questions.q: On a hot day with heavy sweating, the urine produced tends to be:
questions.explanation: Water lost in sweat triggers ADH, so the kidney conserves water and makes little, concentrated urine.

questions.q: Reabsorption is essential because without it the body would:
options: Lose vital water, glucose and salts in the urine
questions.explanation: Reabsorption recovers the useful substances from the 180 L of filtrate, preventing their loss.

questions.q: In haemodialysis, urea moves from the blood into the dialysing fluid by:
options: Diffusion across a selectively permeable membrane
questions.explanation: Urea diffuses down its concentration gradient across the membrane into the waste-free dialysing fluid.

questions.q: Drinking plenty of water helps prevent kidney stones because it:
options: Dilutes the salts so they are less likely to crystallise
questions.explanation: More water keeps salts dissolved and flushed out, reducing the chance of crystals forming.
